name: Dill (Anethum graveolens)
short: Case report titled 'Anaphylaxis to dill': tongue and throat swelling, hives and vomiting after food cooked with dill. In a 91-patient trial, those taking dill tablets reported no side effects.
text: Allergy (case report): a report titled 'Anaphylaxis to dill' describes a patient with allergic rhinitis who developed itching in the mouth, swelling of the tongue and throat, hives, and immediate vomiting and diarrhoea after eating foods cooked with dill, and later on inhaling foods prepared with dill; skin testing with fresh dill was positive, and the authors conclude that dill can cause IgE-mediated (allergic) reactions. This was dill eaten in cooked food; the abstract does not say which part of the plant. Dill taken by mouth in trials: in a 2-month randomised trial in 91 people with high blood lipids comparing dill tablets (the abstract does not say what the tablets contained, such as the plant part, or whether they were powder or extract) with gemfibrozil, patients treated with dill did not report any side effects. In a 6-week single-blind placebo-controlled trial in 150 people with high blood lipids, triglycerides rose by 6.0% in the dill tablet group, which the authors describe as surprising; the abstract gives no significance test for this rise. The trials of dill powder in primary dysmenorrhoea (75 students) and in type 2 diabetes (42 patients) report no adverse-event data, and the dysmenorrhoea trial's authors recommend further study of dill's side effects and interactions. A 2016 Cochrane review of dietary supplements for dysmenorrhoea, which included dill among 12 herbal medicines, found that very few studies reported adverse effects and that evidence of safety is lacking. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
